forces: Chorus and orchestra with trumpets and timpani
performers: London Symphony Orchestra; London Philharmonic Choir; Hermann Scherchen, conductor; Frederick Jackson, chorus master
intro: Handel closes Part II of Messiah with a chorus that can shout together, chase a tune through four voices, or hold one note above the commotion. Hermann Scherchen conducts the London Symphony Orchestra and London Philharmonic Choir.

sections.label: A · Hallelujah in D major
sections.mNote: Strings announce the tune; the choir answers

sections.label: B · The basses take the tune
sections.mNote: “For the Lord” passes between the voices

sections.label: C · King of kings
sections.mNote: Long upper notes above quick choral answers

sections.label: D · And he shall reign again
sections.mNote: The basses bring back the leaping fugue subject

sections.label: A′ · The last Hallelujah
sections.mNote: A pause, then the final G-to-D cadence

cues.title: The strings say it first
cues.text: The first violins already have the rhythm of “Hallelujah”. Three bars later the choir takes up the word, all four parts together. D major, short cries, and little answering runs in the strings: the celebration begins without ceremony.
cues.evidence: Handel, Messiah, Hallelujah, bars 1–7; Joshua Koo’s Mutopia full score, violin and choral parts. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The kingdom of this world
cues.text: The quick cries stop. “The kingdom of this world” moves in measured crotchets, the choir speaking together over a descending bass. Handel leaves room around the words before “the kingdom of our Lord” carries the phrase upwards.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 33–41: choral setting of “The kingdom of this world” and “the kingdom of our Lord”. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The basses start a fugue
cues.text: The basses begin “And he shall reign” with a tune that leaps up and down through the chord. Tenors, altos and sopranos take it in turn. Short “Hallelujah” cries keep returning around the tune.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 41–51: bass entry in bar 41, tenor in 43, alto in 46 and soprano in 48. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Long notes above the choir
cues.text: “King of kings” begins on a held A in the sopranos and altos. The sopranos then climb through D, E, F♯ and G, stretching each proclamation over the busy answers below.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 51–68: sustained A in soprano and alto, followed by the soprano’s ascending proclamations. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A pause before the end
cues.text: The repeated “Hallelujah” cries break off. After the rest, the choir has one last, broad statement of the word. The bass moves from G to D beneath it, and Handel holds the final D major chord under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 92–94: rest, final declaration, G-to-D plagal cadence and fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The basses take “For the Lord”
transitions.to: B · The basses take the tune
transitions.how: The basses take “For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth” on D, rising through E and F♯. The first violins double the tune low in their range, while the sopranos rest. The opening’s four-part shouts separate into a melody and its shorter “Hallelujah” answers.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 17–24: bass and first-violin statement of “For the Lord”, followed by the upper voices. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

transitions.title: An A held above the answers
transitions.from: B · The basses take the tune
transitions.how: The fugue reaches A major. Sopranos and altos stay on A for “King of kings”, holding across the barline; tenors and basses answer with short “Hallelujah” figures. The strings join those quick replies, leaving the long vocal note hanging above them.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 49–56: cadence in A major and sustained upper-voice proclamations over short replies. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

transitions.title: The basses reopen the fugue
transitions.to: D · And he shall reign again
transitions.how: The sopranos release their high G and descend towards E as the choir settles on A major. The basses bring back “And he shall reign”, and the other voices move into the leaping tune again. The first violins join the sopranos’ entry.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 67–74: end of the sustained soprano G, A-major arrival and renewed bass fugue entry in bar 69. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

transitions.title: A rest before the final word
transitions.from: D · And he shall reign again
transitions.how: Choir and orchestra interrupt their repeated “Hallelujah” figures with a rest. The last statement begins in longer notes, and the bass moves from G to D for the plagal cadence. All four voices finish together on the D major chord, held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 90–94: repeated acclamations, rest and the final G-to-D cadence. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

source.title: Handel, Messiah, HWV 56, Hallelujah, full score (Joshua Koo, Mutopia)
source.locator: Joshua Koo’s Mutopia full score and orchestral parts, bars 1–94. The choir begins in bar 4; trumpets and timpani first enter late in bar 14. The closing bars contain the rest, G-to-D cadence and final fermata.

timeline.note: First violins announce the Hallelujah rhythm above the bass; trumpets and timpani rest.
The choir takes the word Hallelujah, with oboes doubling and strings answering.
Trumpets and timpani join the short Hallelujah replies.
The kingdom of this world moves in measured choral crotchets above a descending bass; brass and timpani rest.
Sopranos and altos hold A for King of kings; strings, brass and drums join the short answers below.
The high soprano and trumpet G descends towards E; the basses bring back And he shall reign.
Choir and orchestra pause before the last Hallelujah and its G-to-D cadence.

composer.epithet: He filled London theatres with Italian opera, then put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg offered something noisier: a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant; Prince Ruspoli gave him singers and instrumentalists to write for. The Dixit Dominus of 1707 sends five choral parts racing through a Latin psalm, then makes them hold dissonant notes while the other voices move underneath. His chamber cantatas tried the same arts of persuasion with a single singer. Corelli’s Rome taught him what a violin could say beside a voice.
